jaṭā
(‘matted hair’)
------------------------------------------
In order to be free of the botheration of maintaining the hair, the अस्चेतिच्स् and yogis used to apply some milky exudation of some trees like the banyan and twist the hair into convenient strands and coils. This would prevent dirt and lice from settling on the head and also keep the hair in order.
In iconographical works such matted hair is shown in the case of शिव, some forms of देवी, सुब्रह्मण्य and शास्ता. Depending on the pattern of arrangement of hair, several names are given for the जटा.
In जटामुकुट, the hair is dressed like a crown. Many deities (both gods and goddesses) are shown with this जटामुकुट.
It is called jaṭābandha or jaṭākalāpa when the matted hair is wound round the head and tied as a knot at the top. The sages usually are shown with this type.
In jaṭāmaṇḍala the strands of hair are arranged in a circular halo. Forms of शिव are generally shown with this type.

Jaṭāyu
------------------------------------------
There are not many persons in the history of the world who were prepared to fight and lay down their lives for धर्म or righteousness. And, जटायु the bird-hero, is a glorious and inspiring example that we come across in that immortal epic, the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि.
As per the details given in the Mahābhārata (Ādiparva 67) he and Saṁpāti (his elder brother) were the sons of अरुण and Śyeni. (Aruṇa was the son of विनता and कश्यप, and the elder brother of गरुड, the bird-mount of Lord विष्णु.)
Once सम्पाति and जटायु flew to great heights towards the sun to test their flying powers. Since जटायु was getting exhausted by the hot rays of the sun, सम्पाति spread his wings over him to protect him but got his own wings burnt as a result, and fell down. जटायु started living in the दण्डक forest, but did not know the whereabouts of his brother.
When राम came to the पञ्चवटी area of the forest, to live there, जटायु introduced himself as the friend of his ड़थेर् दशरथ. At राम’s request, जटायु started living in the nearby area.
When रावण was abducting सीता, जटायु ambushed him, fought with him fiercely to rescue सीता but died in the effort.
Rāma, searching for सीता, came across the dying जटायु, got some information about सीता and her abductor and performed his last rites after his death.
See also RĀMĀYAṆA and SAMPĀTI.

jaṭāmukuṭa
(‘hair dressed up as a crown’)
------------------------------------------
Jaṭā means matted hair. मुकुट is a crown. If the matted hair on the head of a deity is dressed up as a crown—especially in some forms of देवी or शिव, कार्त्तिकेय and शास्ता (Ayyappan)—it is called ‘jaṭāmukuṭa’.
